title: The spontaneous generation debate
claimA: Pouchet and supporters argued microbial life could arise spontaneously from decaying organic matter given the right conditions.
claimB: Pasteur argued microorganisms only arise from pre-existing microorganisms, never spontaneously.
evidence: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments (1859-1861) showed sterilized broth stayed lifeless unless exposed to airborne particles.
resolution: The French Academy of Sciences awarded Pasteur the Alhumbert Prize in 1862 for experimentally settling the debate.
modern: Spontaneous generation is considered definitively disproven; all known life arises from prior life.

title: Germ theory versus miasma theory
claimA: Miasma theorists held that disease arose from "bad air" and environmental corruption.
claimB: Germ theorists, building on Koch and Pasteur, held that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.
evidence: Koch's postulates and repeated isolation of disease-specific bacteria (anthrax, tuberculosis, cholera) provided repeatable causal proof.
resolution: By the 1880s-1890s, accumulating bacteriological evidence and public health successes shifted medical consensus toward germ theory.
modern: Germ theory is foundational to modern medicine and microbiology.

title: Semmelweis and the rejection of hand hygiene
claimA: Semmelweis argued invisible "cadaverous particles" carried on doctors' hands caused childbed fever.
claimB: Contemporary physicians rejected the idea that their own unwashed hands could be spreading disease.
evidence: Mortality from childbed fever dropped sharply in Vienna after mandatory hand-washing was introduced in his clinic in 1847.
resolution: Semmelweis's practice was widely rejected in his lifetime; broad acceptance only came decades later once germ theory was established.
modern: Hand hygiene is now a cornerstone of infection control worldwide.

title: Helicobacter pylori and the cause of ulcers
claimA: The medical consensus held that stress and excess stomach acid alone caused gastric ulcers.
claimB: Marshall and Warren argued a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, was the actual cause.
evidence: Marshall drank a culture of H. pylori in 1984 and developed gastritis, and antibiotic treatment was later shown to cure ulcers.
resolution: Clinical trials through the late 1980s and 1990s confirmed antibiotics cured ulcers linked to H. pylori, and medical guidelines changed.
modern: H. pylori is recognized as a leading cause of peptic ulcers and gastric cancer risk; Marshall and Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize.

title: Archaea as a separate domain of life
claimA: Microbiologists traditionally classified all prokaryotes together as "bacteria", including what are now called archaea.
claimB: Carl Woese argued, based on 16S rRNA sequencing, that archaea were as genetically distinct from bacteria as both are from eukaryotes.
evidence: Comparative rRNA sequence analysis published in 1977 showed deep genetic divergence between methanogens and typical bacteria.
resolution: Woese's three-domain classification (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) gradually gained acceptance through the 1980s-1990s as more molecular evidence accumulated.
modern: The three-domain system is now the standard framework in taxonomy, though debate continues over finer details of the tree of life.

title: The priority dispute over penicillin's discovery
claimA: Alexander Fleming is credited with discovering penicillin in 1928 after observing mold killing bacteria on a culture plate.
claimB: French physician Ernest Duchesne had observed similar antibacterial effects of Penicillium mold in an unpublished 1897 thesis, decades earlier.
evidence: Duchesne's thesis documented mold inhibiting bacterial growth, but it received no attention and was never connected to later antibiotic development.
resolution: Fleming's 1928 observation, followed by Florey and Chain's work to purify and mass-produce penicillin in the 1940s, is what led directly to clinical use.
modern: Fleming is conventionally credited with the discovery that launched the antibiotic era, though historians note Duchesne's earlier, disconnected observation.
